Halloween and Singles’ Day, China’s November 11 shopping frenzy, are almost upon us, and acoustics has not slowed down on its way to meeting condensed matter. Following When acoustics meets condensed matter, part 1, jemand brings us the sequel. Pull up a chair and enjoy the show.

Topological structure in solid materials (continued)

3. Band topology and topological insulators

Popular-science articles on topology are legion, and examples like the coffee cup and the doughnut are everywhere, so for reasons of space I won’t repeat them here. Only one point needs stressing: the purpose of studying an object’s topological properties is to find an intrinsic invariance that is immune to outside perturbations. Such invariance is extremely valuable in practice, because nothing real is perfect. Even the purest crystal contains impurities, and its lattice periodicity will be disturbed. Often, to give a material some particular property, you even have to break its lattice periodicity to a degree, and then doping is a must. In electronic band structures, this intrinsic invariance can be described mathematically by topological invariants. There are many ways to define a topological invariant; here I will mention only one, the Chern number, named after the mathematician Shiing-Shen Chern:

The formula is taken from reference [1]. → is called the Berry connection, and its curl is called the Berry phase. There are plenty of popular articles on both, so feel free to look them up on Baidu, Wikipedia or Google. Simply put, these two quantities describe the geometric structure and properties of an object. Take the well-known Foucault pendulum: a simple pendulum ought to keep swinging in the same plane, but because of the curvature of the ground and the Earth’s rotation, that plane slowly rotates. The angle of this rotation is an example of a Berry phase; it reflects the geometry of the space the pendulum lives in. For energy bands, the Berry phase of each level follows from the formula above, given the specific expression for that level.

Figure 6. Foucault pendulum [3]

Integrating the Berry phase gives us a topological invariant, Cn, that characterizes the topology of a band. This Cn does not change when the band changes slightly (such changes usually come from impurities in the crystal). If a band has Cn = 0, it is called topologically trivial; if Cn != 0, it is called topologically nontrivial. A topologically nontrivial band structure gives a material rather special macroscopic properties, and because these properties are tied to topology, they are highly robust: impurities and the material’s macroscopic shape do not affect them. It is worth noting that Cn always comes out as an integer. This follows from the definition of Cn. Some of you may have heard that studying topology is all about “counting holes”: structures with the same number of holes are considered to have the same properties (technically, they are “homeomorphic”). A coffee cup and a doughnut, for instance, each have exactly one hole, so from a topological point of view they are the same thing. You can think of Cn as the number of “holes” in a band structure, only we cannot see them directly. And the number of holes has to be an integer; nobody has ever heard of half a hole.

A topological insulator is a material with a topologically nontrivial band structure. Such materials were first found by Shoucheng Zhang and colleagues in quantum wells made of HgTe and CdTe, and later experiments found the same structure in other materials as well. A defining feature of a topological insulator is that the bands in its interior are topologically trivial, just like those of an ordinary insulator, while its surface hosts a topologically nontrivial band structure. The difference arises because the crystal’s boundary truncates the periodic potential the electrons sit in. Deep inside the crystal, boundary effects can be neglected, but right at the boundary this truncation can give rise to topologically nontrivial bands. Drawing the two kinds of bands together gives the figure below:

Figure 7. Schematic band structure of a topological insulator [2]

The black-and-white bands represent the interior: electrons completely fill the lower, valence band, so this is clearly an insulator. The two lines, one blue and one red, are the levels at the boundary, also known as edge states. Notice that these two lines run across both the conduction band and the valence band, so electrons occupying them can easily be accelerated by an external electric field to produce a macroscopic current. The surface of a topological insulator is therefore, paradoxically, a conductor. Moreover, because of the edge states’ dispersion relation, the direction of the momentum an accelerated electron can acquire is restricted; in two dimensions, this means current flows in one direction only. That is the magic of topological insulators. To stress it once more: because they are topologically protected, these edge states are very stable and unaffected by impurities. Properties like these are thought to offer a way, via the quantum Hall effect, to build components for the long-promised quantum computer.

About the author: jemand graduated in physics from Nanjing University and is now studying for a master’s in physics at RWTH Aachen University. Will probably end up working on something to do with acoustics. That’s all.

[2] X. L. Qi, Rev. Mod. Phys. 83(4), 1057-1110 (2011).
